comments.author: @maxziebell4013
comments.text: I am totally on the side of OpenAI, but there is a nuance to consider regarding statistical correlation and the nature of compression in language models. It's theoretically feasible that, with a sufficient number of tokens, a model could overfit and describe the original content nearly perfectly in a token-compressed way. This is particularly true for famous phrases or lines from well-known works, such as Shakespeare's 'To be, or not to be' or Goethe's 'Faust'. In these cases, the model can indeed replicate these specific phrases. However, when it comes to generating larger, unique content, setting the temperature to near determinism might generate outputs with high relevance, but the likelihood of reproducing an exact copy of unique, longer content is still quite low. This is due to the diversity of the training data and built-in mechanisms to prevent direct copying. Therefore, while language models can echo famous lines, they are primarily designed to generate novel, contextually relevant content rather than replicate extensive passages verbatim. It's an edge case in usage and settings, akin to a savant being an edge case of humanity.

comments.author: @JohnLewis-old
comments.text:
Several key points need clarification:

1. Large Language Models (LLMs) have the capability to reproduce entire books. For example, they can recite the first chapter of "Alice in Wonderland" from memory and then it will continue through the entire book. This demonstrates that LLMs have the ability to act as comprehensive text databases, even though "Alice in Wonderland" is a public domain work and not subject to copyright issues.

2. Addressing the concerns surrounding LLMs and copyright law may not be the most effective approach. The current legal system, based in the concepts of property law, is outdated and struggles to adapt to the concept of protecting ideas under "intellectual property" rights. This approach is often seen as a makeshift solution rather than a robust legal framework.

3. It's important to recognize that individuals who profit from creative works should compensate the original creators. This principle is often overlooked amidst the ongoing discussions about AI. Supporting the creators is crucial, especially as society navigates the shift towards an AI-influenced era. Sam Altman's article on Universal Basic Income (UBI) and Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) offers insights into how society might adapt to these changes.

comments.text: this case is incredibly important. The NYT demanding the deletion of the model is how American copyright law works, and is fully to be expected for their opening salvo. I don't think NYT expects to win their case and have OpenAI delete GPT4, but what I do expect is to finally get a proper line in the sand in the American legal justice system on where and what and how training data can be used and how much that impacts the end product. While I don't think the NYT has too much merit, the fact they were able to reproduce their copyrighted content at all is proof enough that their articles were used for training at some point. We've all kind of been waiting for a case like this to spring up, and now we'll finally get a proper verdict on if this is transformative enough of a resource or not to fall under copyright domain. Also, OpenAI is insisting they trained on public domain, but lets be real, spend 15 mins on /r/news and you'll see "article is paywalled, here's the text:" and while NYT and other big news sites do police the major subreddits for comments like that and have them removed, reddit is gigantic and content like that can still fly under the radar until vacuumed up by a bot for training. This will also be something that needs to be addressed by the courts as well, and it will be interesting (and potentially horrible) to see their decision. still, this is something that will likely take years to worm up to the supreme court if it does get that far.

comments.author: @mickelodiansurname9578
comments.text:
its fairly easy to demonstrate that models don't store the data verbatim... one mathematical, the other demonstrable. So ChatGPT for example will have been trained on lots of public data right? Now when that training was done the SIZE of that text, overall, in terms of words in total, will be somethere between 500 billion to 700 billion words, or at least that the size of the 'common crawl' corpus of text which is in fact available, right now. Its been zipped for anyone to use. But ChatGPT's model is not 500 billion parameters in size let alone 500 billion words, so by definition is cannot contain those words in sequence. Instead it retain pretty much only the embeddings or relationship between those words. So it might have read the word 'Bucket" say a million times... but not all the text that has the word bucket in it is retained in the model just a statistical representation of all the words that appeared around bucket in its training data... So thats the first thing... the model is simply not large enough to have the articles from the new york times, verbatim within the model. The BNYT's lawyers tried to demonstrate something that the engineers in OpenAI knew was not possible.

Next the demonstrable bit and we can do this with things we know it read. ChatGPT has absolutely read moby dick during training. Moby Dick is not under copyright since its over a century old. Yet even so it can remember the first words, and the plotline, but if you ask it to reiterate the first page... well it can't do that... it gets may 20 words in and from there on its starts to lose cohesion as the probability of the next word is swayed in terms of statistical probability by the rest of the times it seen text 'like this' and it deviates. You can try that right now in ChatGPT, as the paragraph goes on the words change until ultimately they are not the same at all as the words in the book and if you keep saying 'continue' at the end of each output it will start making its own story up, hallucinating the storyline based on whats in its context window so far, the further it goes, the more it deviates.

So this claim by NYT really is without merit cos they will not be able to demonstrate even their own examples in a courtroom. And we can test that ourselves using any model... openai or open source they all operate the same.

If NYT and related entities are trying to say that LLMs aren't fair use, they would have to show that it's somehow less transformative than the Google case. comments.text:
Why is everyone so biased against the NYT here? Copyright law is written in the way that they must ask OpenAI to stop what they are doing, they cannot simply asked to be paid. I'm pretty sure that NYT would allow training if they were compensated in a way they think is fair. It also isn't anti-LLM to factually conclude that GPT4 can regurgitate prominent training data very very well. In the past, I asked ChatGPT4 a very specific question about Al Gore's 2000 Concession Speech, and as a follow up I asked if it knew the speech verbatim. It just gave it to me 2/3rds of the way through. It gave more with a little nudging. Clearly it can regurgitate, and even if it is rare, that still is copyright infringement.

Sure, maybe it is indeed "rare", and I also think that the ancient ways copyright laws work should not prohibit this technological development. But I don't see how it makes sense to argue that GPT4 doesn't contain the copyrighted material that it clearly contains, and I don't see how it makes sense to claim that what OpenAI is doing is clairly fair use. Fair use is pretty broad and needs to be evaluated in context, so I do think it is a legitimate open question whether this actually is fair use. Maybe a precedent will be set that training is indeed fair use if regurgitation is sufficiently blocked. Maybe a precedent will be set that training isn't allowed at all. Or maybe a precedent will be set that training is only allowed for models small enough that they cannot possibly regurgitate.

I'm certainly rooting for OpenAI here, but I don't think NYT is doing anything wrong, they are just protecting what they think are their IP rights in an area of law that does not yet have precedent.

comments.text:
I've liked a lot of your content, but this feels so far off the mark. Maybe this is something you've thought through a lot and come to a conclusion on, but it feels like a bias you're holding due to how closely tied your income streams are to AI. 

Whether or not training AI with information freely (or not freely) available on the internet constitutes fair use has massive ethical implications, not the least of which is content creators' future income streams - should a content creator not be entitled to "license" their intellectual property for use in AI training, or to refuse to sell such a license as they see fit? You mention this toward the end of the video, but these deals are only made with large publishers. The average person whose content has been used gets nothing. 

OpenAI has shown they don't really care about these ethical implications in any way that matters. Case in point: the DALL-E training opt-out mechanism. Not only does it assume they have the right to everyone's content as the default, but even those artists who request to remove their content can only do so for FUTURE versions of the model. Any money they've made and will continue to make on both current and previous versions of a model, will still belong to OpenAI with no recompense to the artists.

Furthermore, they have advised people to enter URLs they don't want used to train their models into a robots.txt file - which doesn't prevent the image from appearing on other sites where the image would still be scraped from. A more equitable approach would be a similar type of site data like an "AI.txt" and "noAI.txt" file - anything in the AI.txt file incurring the specified licensing rate per page in the file if used for training, everything in noAI.txt explicitly denied as training data, and everything else allowed without charge. All of this still doesn't solve the general issue that most creators won't have a clue how to implement any of it - which is also true for robots.txt files. 

And if the response to this is "it would cost AI companies too much to pay people for the right to use all those sites as training data", then congratulations - you're starting to get why they aren't interested in doing things in an equitable way. 

If the companies bringing these suits had no idea how these models worked (at least at a surface level) they would simply be asking for their specific data to be removed from the models - which can't happen due to the way they are trained, as you explain in your video. That is where the drive to delete the model itself comes from - because you can't pick and choose which training data current and past models are using to generate prompts today. 

The contention is that using their content to train the model is not "fair use". To me at least, this is especially valid when OpenAI who are a (partially) nonprofit organization are raking in massive profits. 

AI absolutely is a powerful and potentially beneficial tool, but the revenues gained through the creation of these AI models absolutely could not exist if not for the original works the models were trained on. Labor, copyright, and intellectual property for which OpenAI has not paid anyone. 

It would be one thing if they were a purely research-based non profit whose sole aim was to further AI research, but when you have revenue over a billion dollars it's pretty hard to say with a straight face that they are working “to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity.” - they're benefiting themselves and shareholders of the for-profit portion of their structure, not the people who created and continue to create the works their models rely on. 

The fact that AI is merely a tool does not make it morally neutral by default. There are a lot of other YouTubers who discuss this, including the videos below. I highly encourage you to give them a watch to gain a broader perspective on this.

- Dr Fatima's "What Succession Tells Us About the Tech Industry"
- PhilosophyTube's "Data" and "A Man Plagiarised My Work: Women, Money, and the Nation"
- Wireless Philosophy's 'Is Technology as “Neutral” as We Think It Is?' for some other perspectives on this.

comments.text:
Correction: it hasn't yet been tested in a court of law whether LLMS actually store the information they injest or not.
A recent paper (see note below) demonstrated that you can extract training data from Production LLMs.

So from the court's perspective if it can be demonstrated that you can get out the exact data that you put in (or near enough) then the data is being "stored" within the model itself.

This is ultimately what this NYT case will determine.

Think of MP3 vs CD Audio as an example. The data format is completely diffetent but because the MP3 can be used to reproduce the original work to a reasonable degree, converting from CD/Wav to MP3 is still considered copying and storing.

Footnote: the paper itself is called: Scalable Extraction of Training Data from (Production) Language Models
